ποίμνην τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἐπι σκόπους ἑαυτοῖς χειροτονοῦντες, πρεσβυτέρους, δια
κόνους, διδασκάλους, λαὸν, κατηχουμένους, μιμού μενοι τὰ αἰώνια πρόβατα,
πληροῦσι τό· Μένουσι δὲ ὡς πρόβατα αἰώνια. Οὐκ εἰσὶ δὲ πρόβατα αἰώνια, ἀλλὰ
μένουσιν ὡς πρόβατα αἰώνια. 17.80 Στίχ. ιαʹ. Τὰ δὲ παιδία αὐτῶν προσπαίζουσι. Στίχ.
ιβʹ. Ἀναλαβόντες ψαλτήριον καὶ κιθάραν. Οἱ ἡμέτεροι ἀναλαμβάνουσι ψαλτήριον
καὶ κιθά ραν, ὑμνοῦντες τὸν Θεὸν, καὶ δοξολογοῦντες αὐτόν. Ἐκείνων δὲ τὰ παιδία,
οἱ ἀνόητοι ἐν αὑτοῖς, προσ παίζουσιν, ἀναλαμβάνοντες ψαλτήριον καὶ κι θάραν. Ὅτ'
ἂν ἀναλάβωσι τοὺς λόγους τῆς Παλαιᾶς ∆ιαθήκης, προσπαίζουσι, καὶ γελῶσι τὰ
λόγια τοῦ νόμου καὶ τῶν προφητῶν. Ἀναλαμβάνοντες τὰ ἐναρ μόνια, ψαλτήριον τὸ
τοῦ νόμου, κιθάραν τὴν προφη τικὴν, προσπαίζουσιν αὐτοῖς. Στίχ. ιβʹ. Καὶ
εὐφραίνονται φωνῇ ψαλμοῦ. Καὶ αὐτοὶ λέγουσιν ψαλμοὺς Οὐαλεντίνου, καὶ λέ
γουσιν ᾠδὰς Βασιλείδου, καὶ τοιαῦτά τινα φθέγγον ται, εὐφραινόμενοι φωνῇ
ψαλμοῦ. Στίχ. ιγʹ. Ἐν δὲ ἀναπαύσει ᾅδου ἐκοιμήθησαν. Ἐν δὲ ἀναπαύσει οὐκ
οὐρανοῦ, ἀλλ' ᾅδου ἐκοιμή θησαν. Ἡμεῖς δὲ εὐχόμεθα οὐκ ἐν ἀναπαύσει ᾅδου
κοιμηθῆναι, ἀλλ' ἐν ἀναπαύσει Θεοῦ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς τοῖς ἁγίοις μετὰ Χριστοῦ
βασιλεύοντος ἡμῶν· ᾧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.
ΚΕΦ. ΚΒʹ. Στίχ. βʹ. Πότερον οὐχὶ Κύριός ἐστιν ὁ διδά σκων σύνεσιν καὶ ἐπιστήμην; Τὰ
οἰκονομούμενα ὑπὸ τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος ἀνα γραφῆς ἀξιωθῆναι χρή. ∆ιὰ τοῦτο
ἀναγράφεται ὑπὲρ τοῦ τὸν ἐντυγχάνοντα ὠφελεῖσθαι ἐκ τῶν ἀναγινω σκομένων. Εἰ
μὴ οὖν χρήσιμοι ἦσαν οἱ λόγοι τῶν τριῶν, τῶν παραγενομένων πρὸς τὸν Ἰὼβ, ὡς
τὸν ἐντυγχάνοντα λαβεῖν τι ἀπὸ τῶν εἰρημένων ὑπ' αὐτῶν πρὸς τὸν Ἰώβ· οὐκ ἂν ἡ
πρόνοια εἰς τὴν βίβλον τοῦ Ἰὼβ ἐποίησεν ἀναγραφῆναι καὶ τοὺς λόγους τῶν τριῶν.
Ἔστιν οὖν ὠφεληθῆναι μὲν ἀπὸ τῶν λόγων αὐτοῦ, ἐνορῶντα τοῖς δόγμασιν· ὁρᾷν δὲ
τὸ ἔγκλη τον τῶν λόγων περὶ ἓν μόνον, ὅτε αἰτιῶνται τὸν Ἰὼβ, οἰόμενοι αὐτὸν
πάσχειν διὰ τὰ ἡμαρτημένα αὐτῷ· οὐχ ὁρῶντες, ὅτι καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ αἴτιά ἐστι τοῦ
συμ βαίνειν ἀνθρώποις. Τοιαῦτά ἐστι νενομισμένα εἶναι καλὰ ἢ χαλεπὰ, ἢ ὅπως ποτὲ
βούλεταί τις αὐτὰ ὀνομάζειν. Καὶ μετ' ὀλίγα· Πότερον οὐχὶ ὁ Κύ ριός ἐστιν ὁ
διδάσκων σύνεσιν καὶ ἐπιστήμην; Τὸ δόγμα ὑγιές ἐστι· ὅτι ἀληθινὸς διδάσκαλος
ἀρετῆς οὐ δύναται εἶναι ἄνθρωπος. Ὁ διδάσκων γὰρ ἄνθρωπον γνῶσιν, καὶ ἐν τοῖς
Ψαλμοῖς ἀναγέ γραπται, ὅτι οὐκ ἄλλος ἐστὶν ἢ Θεός. Καὶ, ∆ίδαξόν με, φησὶν, τὰ
δικαιώματά σου, ὁ Προφήτης, εἰδὼς δι δάσκαλον εἶναι ἀληθῆ καὶ τέλειον τὸν Θεόν.
∆ιδά σκει δὲ ὁ Θεὸς ἐλλάμπων τῇ ψυχῇ τοῦ μανθάνοντος ὑπ' αὐτοῦ, καὶ τὴν
διάνοιαν φωτίζων τῷ φωτὶ, τῷ ἀληθινῷ λόγῳ αὐτοῦ. Οὐκοῦν καὶ ἄνδρες δίκαιοι
ἡμᾶς διδάσκουσι διδασκαλικὴν εἰληφότες χάριν. Στίχ. δʹ. Καὶ συνεισελεύσεταί σοι εἰς
κρίσιν. Λόγον ποιούμενος ὁ Θεὸς τοῦ προνοουμένου ὑπ' αὐ τοῦ, ἐλέγχει αὐτόν. Καὶ
συνεισελεύσεταί σοι εἰς κρίσιν. Πολλάκις εἴπομεν, εἴποτε ἐνέπεσε τὸ δόγμα 17.81
τοῦτο ἐν ἄλλαις λέξεσιν, ὅτι οὕτως ἐστὶν ὁ Θεὸς φιλ άνθρωπος, ὥστε, καὶ χρηστῶς
κρίνων ἡμᾶς, ἐπι τρέπει λέγειν ἡμᾶς πρὸς αὐτὸν, ὡς κρινόμενον μεθ' ἡμῶν, περὶ ὧν
βουλόμεθα. Ἐχρησάμην οὖν τοῖς ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἡσαΐα· ∆εῦτε, καὶ διαλεχθῶμεν, λέγει Κύ
ριος. Τὸ γὰρ, διαλεχθῶμεν, τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν· Εἴ τί με ἔχεις ἐλέγξαι, καὶ τὴν πρόνοιάν
μου, ὡς ἀμελή σαντός σου, ὡς μὴ τὰ δέοντα πεποιηκότος, λέγε· Κἀγὼ, ὅ τι ποτὲ ἔχω
ἐρῶ, πείσω σε, καταδικάζων σε ἄξιον ὄντα τοῦ καταδικασθῆναι. Στίχ. εʹ. Πότερον
οὐχ ἡ κακία σου ἐστὶ πολλή; Εἰκότως οὐχ ἁπλῶς φημι γεγονέναι ἄδικον· ἐπεὶ πάσχει
τοιαῦτα, ὁποῖα οὐδεὶς αὐτῶν τηλικούτοις πέπτωκεν, οἵοις σύ. Εἰκὸς διὰ τὸ
ἀναρίθμητόν σου τῶν πταισμάτων, ταῦτά σοι ἐληλυθέναι. Τοῦ αὐτοῦ. Οὐ πρότερον
ὠνόμασεν ἁμαρτίαν, εἶτα τὴν κακίαν· ἀλλ' ὁρῶν τὴν κακίαν τὴν φαύλην ἕξιν, εἶτα
μετὰ τοῦτο τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς φαύλης ἕξεως ἁμαρτανόμενα, ἅπερ εἶπεν ἀναριθμήτους εἶναι
ἁμαρ τίας. Στίχ. εʹ. Ἀναρίθμητοι δέ σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι. Ὑπολαμβάνει τοῦτο ὁ Ἐλιφὰζ
περὶ τοῦ Ἰώβ. Ἤδει αὐτὸν πλούσιον, καί φησιν· Ἐνέχυρα ἐλάμβανες ἀπὸ τῶν σῶν
ἀδελφῶν, ὡς ὀφειλόντων μὴ ὀφειλόντων. Τὸ γὰρ, Ἠνεχύραζες διακενῆς, τοιοῦ τόν
ἐστιν. Στίχ. ʹ. Ἠνεχύραζες τοὺς ἀδελφούς σου διακενῆς. Τοῦ αὐτοῦ. Προσεπιτείνει δὲ
πάλιν ἄλλην αὐτοῦ ἁμαρτίαν. Ἔστι ποτὲ λαβεῖν ἀμφιάσματα; Οὐ γυμ νοῦ, ἀλλὰ
πλουσίου ἔχοντος ἀποκείμενα ἐνδύματα πολλὰ λαβεῖν. Τρία ... δὴ ὁ τῶν πολλῶν
pass_a_gloss: ...flock of Christ, ordaining for themselves overseers, elders, deacons, teachers, people, catechumens, imitating the eternal sheep, they fulfil the: and they remain like eternal sheep. But they are not eternal sheep, but they remain like eternal sheep. Verse 11. And their children play toward. Verse 12. Having taken up psaltery and harp. Ours take up psaltery and harp, hymning God and glorifying him. But the children of those, the senseless in themselves, play toward, taking up psaltery and harp. Whenever they take up the words of the Old Covenant, they play toward and laugh at the oracles of the law and the prophets. Taking up the harmonious things, the psaltery that of the law, the harp the prophetic one, they play toward them. Verse 12. And they are glad at a voice of psalm. And they themselves say psalms of Valentinus, and say odes of Basilides, and utter some such things, being glad at a voice of psalm. Verse 13. And in rest of Hades they fell asleep. In rest, not of heaven, but of Hades they fell asleep. But we pray not to sleep in rest of Hades, but in rest of God in the holy heavens with Christ reigning over us; to whom the glory and the might into the ages of the ages. Amen. Chapter 22, verse 2. Is not the Lord the one teaching understanding and knowledge? The things administered by the Holy Spirit must be deemed worthy of writing up. Because of this it is written up for the one reading to be benefited from the things read. If then the words of the three, those having come to Job, were not useful, so that the reader take something from the things said by them to Job, providence would not have made also the words of the three be written up into the book of Job. It is possible then to be benefited from his words, looking into the doctrines; and to see the blameworthy of the words about one only, when they accuse Job, supposing him to suffer through the things sinned by him; not seeing that also many other things are causes of the happening to men. Such are the things held to be fine or hard, or however someone wants to name them. And after a little: Is not the Lord the one teaching understanding and knowledge? The doctrine is healthy: that a true teacher of virtue cannot be a man. For the one teaching man knowledge, also in the Psalms it is written up, that it is not another than God. And: teach me your ordinances, says the Prophet, knowing God to be teacher true and perfect. God teaches by shining on the soul of the one learning under him, and illuminating the mind with the light, his true Word. Therefore also righteous men teach us, having received a teaching grace. Verse 4. And he will go in with you into judgement. Making account, God, of the one provided for by him, refutes him. And he will go in with you into judgement. Often we said, if ever this doctrine fell in in other wordings, that God is so man-loving that, even judging us kindly, he permits us to speak toward him, as one being judged with us, about whatever we want. I used then the things from Isaiah: come, and let us converse, says the Lord. For the 'let us converse' is such: if you have anything to refute me, and my providence, as having neglected you, as not having done the needful things, speak; and I, whatever I have, will say, I will persuade you, condemning you as being worthy to be condemned. Verse 5. Is not your wickedness much? Reasonably I say you have not simply become unjust; since he suffers such things as none of them has fallen into such great ones as you. It is likely that through the countlessness of your stumbles these things have come to you. Of the same. He did not first name sin, then the wickedness; but seeing the wickedness, the bad habit, then after this the things sinned from the bad habit, which he said to be countless sins. Verse 5. And your sins are countless. Eliphaz supposes this about Job. He knew him rich, and says: you took pledges from your brothers as owing, not owing. For the 'you took pledges for nothing' is such. Verse (number lost). You took pledges of your brothers for nothing. Of the same. And he again further stretches another sin of his. Is it possible ever to take garments? Not of a naked one, but of a rich one having stored-away clothes many to take. Three ... indeed the of the many...
pass_b_english: … flock of Christ, appointing for themselves bishops, presbyters, deacons, teachers, a laity and catechumens, they imitate the everlasting sheep and so fulfil the words: “They remain like everlasting sheep” (Job 21:11). But they are not everlasting sheep; they only remain like everlasting sheep.

“And their children make sport” (Job 21:11). “Taking up psaltery and harp” (Job 21:12). Our people take up psaltery and harp to sing hymns to God and give him glory. But the children of those men, senseless as they are within themselves, make sport as they take up psaltery and harp. Whenever they take up the words of the Old Testament, they make sport of them and laugh at the oracles of the Law and the Prophets. They take up the instruments that are in tune, the psaltery of the Law and the harp of prophecy, and make sport with them.

“And they rejoice at the sound of a psalm” (Job 21:12). They too recite psalms, the psalms of Valentinus, and recite odes, the odes of Basilides, and they utter things of that kind, rejoicing at the sound of a psalm.

“And in the rest of Hades they fell asleep” (Job 21:13). In rest, yes, but not the rest of heaven: it was in the rest of Hades that they fell asleep. But we pray to fall asleep not in the rest of Hades but in the rest of God, in the holy heavens, with Christ reigning over us. To him be the glory and the power for ever and ever. Amen.

“Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge?” (Job 22:2). What the Holy Spirit arranges must be counted worthy of being written down. That is why it is written: so that the reader may profit from what he reads. So if the words of the three who came to Job had not been useful, so that the reader could take something from what they said to Job, providence would not have had the words of the three written into the book of Job as well. One may, then, profit from his words by looking closely at the doctrines, and see that what is blameworthy in the words concerns one thing only: they blame Job, thinking that he suffers because of the sins he has committed, and they do not see that there are many other causes of what happens to people. Such are the things that are reckoned good or hard, or whatever name one cares to give them.

And a little later: “Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge?” The doctrine is sound: a human being cannot be a true teacher of virtue. For it is also written in the Psalms that the one who teaches man knowledge is no other than God (Psalm 94:10). And the Prophet says, “Teach me your just decrees” (Psalm 119:12), because he knows that God is the true and perfect teacher. God teaches by shining into the soul of the one who learns from him and by lighting up his mind with the light, his true Word. So righteous men too teach us, when they have received the grace of teaching.

“And he will enter into judgement with you” (Job 22:4). God, taking account of the one he cares for, reproves him. “And he will enter into judgement with you.” We have often said, whenever this doctrine came up in other words, that God loves mankind so much that, even as he judges us kindly, he allows us to speak to him about whatever we wish, as though he were on trial with us. So I used the words of Isaiah: “Come, and let us reason together, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1:18). For “let us reason together” means something like this: If you have any charge to bring against me and my providence, as though I had neglected you, as though I had not done what was needed, speak. And I will say whatever I have to say, and I will persuade you, condemning you as one who deserves to be condemned.

“Is not your wickedness great?” (Job 22:5). With good reason, I say, you have not simply been unjust; for he suffers things such as none of them has fallen into, things as great as yours. It is likely that these things have come upon you because your faults are past counting.

From the same: He did not name sin first and then wickedness. Rather, he looked at wickedness as the bad state of the soul, and after that at the sins committed from that bad state, which he said are sins past counting.

“And your sins are past counting” (Job 22:5). Eliphaz supposes this about Job. He knew that he was rich, and he says: You took pledges from your brothers as though they owed you, when they did not. For that is what “you took pledges for nothing” means. “You took pledges from your brothers for nothing” (Job 22:6).

From the same: Again he presses on to another sin of his. Is it ever possible to take clothing? Not from a naked man, but from a rich man who has many garments laid away. Three … then, the one of the many …
